title: Fruit-fly lines with more nuclear DNA did not develop more slowly or grow larger in independent studies of one natural population; a link with lower survival is inconclusive
abstract: Inbred lines of one natural fruit-fly population that have more nuclear DNA did not develop more slowly or grow larger in experiments by other laboratories. This matters because one proposed function of non-coding ("junk") DNA is a bulk effect: more DNA gives larger, slower-dividing cells and slower development (the nucleotype hypothesis), and a 2014 study reported genome-size effects on development, pupal mass and survival in this population. We used published flow-cytometry genome sizes of 208 lines of the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (mean 175.5 Mb; standard deviation 1.5%) and line means from DGRPool, a public collection of phenotype data. We adjusted for chromosome inversions and Wolbachia infection, combined studies by random-effects meta-analysis, and resampled lines across all studies together (bootstrap), because the studies share lines. A partial correlation is the correlation that remains after this adjustment. In 9 studies of development time, the pooled partial correlation with log genome size was -0.03 (95% CI -0.10 to 0.06), against about +0.19 expected if development time were proportional to DNA content; 1% more DNA lengthens development by at most about 0.3%. In 11 studies of body or organ size it was 0.03 (-0.08 to 0.11). The development interval does not overlap the strongest development effect of the original study after conversion to the whole-panel range of genome size. Survival to adult gave -0.04 (-0.16 to 0.11) in 7 studies (a test added after we saw the original data), but one large study and an averaged survival score were negative, so a weak link is possible. Across 1,802 phenotypes, genome size was not more connected to other traits than random heritable traits were. In 20 lines chosen for small or large wing cells, the large-cell lines did not have more DNA. Limits: genome size varies little within the population, we could not check the flow-cytometry values against sequence data, an earlier analysis of the same genome sizes had already found small trait correlations, and data on cell size and metabolic rate are few.
